children: By Karin Strohecker

Angola is seeking to open its $18.6 billion domestic government bond market to foreign investors, Finance Minister Vera Daves de Sousa told Reuters, as the oil producer looks to broaden its funding base and deepen local capital markets.

As part of the plan, the government is in talks with JPMorgan over potential inclusion in a new frontier market local currency debt index, she said, and would meet international investors in Luanda later this month to gauge demand as it develops a framework for broader market access.
"We want to see if we can gain scale, but for that to happen we need to have a clear channel," she said, speaking in London on the sidelines of an investor conference.

Daves de Sousa added authorities were in contact with JPMorgan, which is preparing to launch a frontier-markets local-currency debt index that could provide investors with a new benchmark for the asset class.
"We are in a close dialogue regarding how we can better explore the potential that the local bond market has for the investors," she said.

For emerging market governments, foreign participation is a way to deepen domestic bond markets, help broaden the investor base, reduce dependence on dollar borrowing and potentially lower government funding costs.

Angola had 17 trillion kwanzas ($18.6 billion) of domestic government debt outstanding by end-2025, according to Finance Ministry data. By comparison, Kenya, whose economy is slightly bigger than Angola's, had the equivalent of nearly three times as much outstanding in domestic government debt.

While foreign investors can already buy Angolan debt, purchases of government securities require central bank approval and local banking arrangements, limiting broader participation by international portfolio investors.

Angola is seeking to tap into a growing pool of investors focused on frontier-market local-currency debt. JPMorgan's planned benchmark - expected to feature Angola's peers such as Nigeria and Kenya - reflects rising investor interest in an asset class long considered difficult to access, as governments work to develop domestic capital markets and reduce dependence on hard-currency borrowing.

Asked about borrowing plans on international capital markets, Daves de Sousa said the government could sell more bonds next year and was considering issuing in other currencies outside the U.S. dollar, including the Chinese yuan.
"If we see the market's condition there in 2027, we will be more than keen to step in," she said.

The government is broadening the tax base, while cutting spending was harder, she said. The government is prioritising growth-boosting investments in power, electricity transmission, water and transport infrastructure.
Angola's debt-to-GDP ratio, including state-owned enterprise debt, is projected to fall to 48% by end-2027 from 54% at end-Q2, she said.
Angola is also exploring a debt-for-nutrition swap with UNICEF, though discussions remain at an early stage.
On fuel prices, Daves de Sousa said the focus was on ensuring adequate supply and expanding cash-transfer programmes to shield vulnerable households, rather than raising prices again.
She said Angola was unlikely to eliminate fuel subsidies within the next year.
Daves De Sousa said the government was likely to raise its 2027 oil-price assumption from the current $61 per barrel, while maintaining a conservative forecasting approach.
The government would continue pushing diversification, though oil revenue was expected to exceed non-oil revenue again in 2027 after a temporary reversal in 2026.

On production, she said Angola was working to keep oil output above 1 million barrels per day. Output averaged 1.04 million bpd at end-Q2, with 2027 production expected to be "something slightly less than this."($1 = 912.8430 kwanzas)($1 = 129.3000 Kenyan shillings)
